# Introduction


This vignette states which covariance DeCovarT needs from a single-cell
reference, and how it is estimated. The target is the within-type
covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ that enters the likelihood, not
a biologically interpretable gene regulatory network. The plug-in is
the linear shrinkage of the empirical covariance
(@sec-cov-shrinkage). Four alternatives are kept as **sensitivity
analyses** of that choice: three sparse-precision estimators (graphical
lasso, `SILGGM` support with a refit, `PLNnetwork`) and a denoised
version of the shrinkage (@sec-raw-vs-denoised). All five are scored by
the same nested cross-validation (@sec-cov-cv), and their effect on the
proportions is measured in the misspecification sweep of the
reproducibility book. The application to the Suppinger gastruloid
reference (gene panel, cell counts, solver settings, outputs) is in
the [covariance chapter of the reproducibility book](https://github.com/bastienchassagnol/DeCovarT_reproducibility/blob/main/docs/03-covariance-estimation.qmd).


::: {#nte-cov-why .callout-note collapse="true" title="Why a regularised covariance rather than a sparse precision"}

DeCovarT evaluates a Gaussian likelihood whose covariance is a sum of
cell-type covariances. With one single-cell specimen, the identified
object is the within-type cell-to-cell covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$, which enters linearly in $p_{ji}$
([one-replicate regime](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-one-replicate)).
With purified population profiles, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ enters
through $\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$
([convolution](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#eq-gaussian-convolution)).
Three arguments favour the covariance as the estimated object. They do
not carry the same weight.

- **Marginalisation (exact).** If the cells of type $j$ have covariance
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ over all genes, the covariance of a panel
  $\mathcal{P}$ is the sub-matrix
  $(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}}$, whatever other genes
  are measured. The precision of the panel is
  $\{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}}\}^{-1}$, a Schur
  complement of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$, not the sub-matrix
  $(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j)_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{P}}$. Removing one gene
  $u$ from the panel changes the remaining entries to

  $$
  \omega'_{gg'}=\omega_{gg'}-\frac{\omega_{gu}\,\omega_{g'u}}{\omega_{uu}} ,
  $$ {#eq-schur-update}

  <!-- chk: V39 -->
  so a precision entry, and the conditional variance $1/\omega_{gg}$,
  change exactly when both genes are neighbours of $u$; the covariance
  entries do not change. A covariance entry is a property of a gene
  pair; a precision entry is a property of the panel. The consequence
  for the prior: regulators outside the panel, including genes removed
  by the feature selection, fill in the panel precision. A few such
  latent variables make the marginal precision sparse plus low rank
  rather than sparse [@chandrasekaranLatentVariableGraphical2012], so a
  sparse $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ on a selected panel is a weak
  assumption.
- **The mixture discards the zeros (generic).** Sums such as
  $\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ or
  $\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ have dense inverses even when
  every $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ is sparse, outside special cases such
  as diagonal $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$. The likelihood uses each
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ only through the sum, which it then inverts.
- **Variance against bias (depends on the truth).** A sparse
  $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ has $|E_j|+G$ free parameters instead of
  $G(G+1)/2$. That lowers the variance when the truth is sparse in
  $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ and adds bias when it is not. The inverse
  matters for DeCovarT: Stein's loss (@prp-gaussian-logscore) weighs
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ as well as $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. The
  question is which object carries the structural assumption, not
  whether the inverse is used.

The same choice is standard for Gaussian plug-in classifiers, whose
discriminant is a likelihood with an estimated covariance. Regularised
discriminant analysis shrinks each class covariance towards a pooled or
diagonal target
[TODO-cite: Friedman 1989, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 84(405):165–175, doi:10.1080/01621459.1989.10478752; not in Zotero]{.highlight}.
In high dimension, the diagonal plug-in ("naive Bayes") can beat the
sample-covariance plug-in of Fisher's linear discriminant
[TODO-cite: Bickel & Levina 2004, Bernoulli 10(6):989–1010, doi:10.3150/bj/1106314847; not in Zotero]{.highlight}.
Warton tunes a ridge-regularised correlation matrix by cross-validated
normal likelihood, the criterion of @sec-cov-cv
[TODO-cite: Warton 2008, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 103(481):340–349, doi:10.1198/016214508000000021; not in Zotero]{.highlight}.
These results support a regularised covariance for prediction. None
shows that it beats a sparse precision when the truth is sparse in
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$; that is why the sparse estimators stay as
sensitivity analyses. The zeros of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ and their
recovery (@sec-cov-regimes, layer 3) matter for a network, not for the
deconvolution. When the proportions are known, `CSNet` estimates
type-level co-expression from the same convolution
([CSNet](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-csnet))
[@suEstimatingCellTypeSpecificGene2024].

:::

| Estimator | Role | Data it sees | Tuning parameter | Object exported to DeCovarT | Graph |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shrinkage, target D (@sec-cov-shrinkage) | plug-in | raw per-cell counts | $\lambda\in[0,1]$; closed-form $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ as start | dense $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$, variances kept | none |
| Denoised shrinkage (@sec-raw-vs-denoised) | sensitivity | raw counts, moment-corrected | $\lambda$; $\kappa$ bracketed, not tuned | dense $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j$ | none |
| Graphical lasso, unpenalised diagonal (@sec-cov-glasso) | sensitivity | correlation $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ of the counts | $\lambda$ | $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{R}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{1/2}$ | support of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j$ |
| `SILGGM` after the nonparanormal map (@sec-cov-npn) | sensitivity | nonparanormal scores | FDR level $\alpha$ | linear-scale refit under the zeros of the support | FDR-controlled support |
| `PLNnetwork` (@sec-cov-pln) | sensitivity | raw UMIs, offset $\log s_c$ | $\lambda$ | linear moments of the latent $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_z,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z)$ (@eq-pln-linear) | support of the latent precision |

: Five estimators of the within-type covariance. The three sparse estimators target *direct* interactions (non-zero partial correlations); the two shrinkage estimators keep direct and indirect associations. Each has one tuned parameter, chosen by the criterion of @sec-cov-cv. {#tbl-cov-estimators}


{{< pagebreak >}}

## Which covariance: raw or denoised {#sec-raw-vs-denoised}

The empirical covariance of raw UMI counts mixes biological covariation
with two measurement terms. This section separates them, states which
of them the bulk inherits, and gives one preprocessing step for every
estimator of @tbl-cov-estimators.

### Measurement model and unknown terms {#sec-cov-unknowns}

A reference cell $c$ of type $j$ is counted as
([Poisson measurement](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#eq-poisson-measurement))

$$
x_{gc}\mid s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c,\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}
\sim\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c\,b_g\,m_{gc}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c},
$$ {#eq-cov-measurement}

with $s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c$, $s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$ and
$\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}$ independent. The unknown terms are:

- $s_c=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_cs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$, the size factor of cell
  $c$: a dimensionless, cell-wide factor. $s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c$ is
  biological (cell volume, cycle phase), $s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$ technical
  (capture efficiency, sequencing depth of the droplet).
- $\nu=\operatorname{CV}^{2}(s_c)$, the extrinsic noise, and its two
  parts $\nu^{\mathrm{bio}}$ and $\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}$.
- $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}$, the size-free expression, with
  covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j$ within type $j$. It is
  the mean of the Poisson measurement once $s_c$ and $b_g$ are factored
  out, proportional to the molecule content $\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}$
  [@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021;
  @fangExtrinsicBiologicalStochasticity2025]. It is not a
  transcription rate in the sense of kinetic models of bursting, in
  which the molecule count is itself random given the rates
  [TODO-cite: Gorin & Pachter, biophysical models of transcription and sequencing (Monod); key not in inst/REFERENCES.bib]{.highlight}.
- $b_g$, the capture efficiency of gene $g$, with
  $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b})$.
- $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\mid j]$
  and $S_j=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$, the mean
  and the mean transcriptome size of a type-$j$ cell, in counts.
- $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j$, the covariance of the captured
  content at unit technical factor, and its mixture
  $\boldsymbol{S}^{\mathrm{bio}}(\boldsymbol{p})$:

  $$
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j
  =\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}\mid j\bigr)
  =(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})\,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}
  +\nu^{\mathrm{bio}}\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top},
  \qquad
  \boldsymbol{S}^{\mathrm{bio}}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_jp_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j .
  $$ {#eq-sigma-bio}

  It keeps the biological size; it is what the
  [denoised within-type covariance](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#eq-denoised-within)
  estimates.
- $a_i$, $c_i=a_in_i$ and $\phi_i=a_i^{2}n_i$, the bulk scales: $a_i$
  is the bulk depth per cell relative to the reference, $n_i$ the number
  of cells behind bulk sample $i$.

### Size factors: what they are and how they relate {#sec-cov-size-factors}

**Why $\mathbb{E}[s_c\mid j]=1$.** @eq-cov-measurement depends on the
cell factors only through the product $s_c\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}$:
for any $k>0$, the pair $(ks_c,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}/k)$ gives
the same law. The scale of $s_c$ is not identified, and one constraint
per type fixes it, as in Fang and Pachter (their equations 1–2):
$\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c\mid j]=\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c\mid j]=1$.
By independence,

$$
\mathbb{E}[s_c\mid j]=\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c]\,\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c]=1,
\qquad
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\,\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}\mid j],
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[x_{+c}\mid s_c,j]=s_c\,S_j ,
$$ {#eq-size-factor-mean}

so the type-level size goes into the mean, and the size factor is the
library rescaled by it. Its plug-in estimate
$\hat s_c=x_{+c}\big/\bigl(C_j^{-1}\sum_{c'\in j}x_{+c'}\bigr)$ has mean
exactly one over the cells of type $j$.
<!-- chk: V37a, V37b -->

**Why $1+\nu=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}})$.** With
$\mathbb{E}[s_c]=1$, $\nu=\operatorname{Var}(s_c)/\mathbb{E}[s_c]^{2}=\mathbb{E}[s_c^{2}]-1$,
and the same holds for each factor. Independence of the two factors
gives

$$
1+\nu=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c)^{2}\bigr]\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[(s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c)^{2}\bigr]
=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}),
\qquad
\nu=\nu^{\mathrm{bio}}+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}}\nu^{\mathrm{tech}} .
$$ {#eq-extrinsic-product}

<!-- chk: V37c -->
The identity needs $s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c$ independent of
$s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$. A capture efficiency that grows with cell volume
would break it.

**$S_j$ against $s_c$.** The two are different objects. $S_j$ is a
type-level mean transcriptome size, in counts; $s_c$ is a within-type,
dimensionless fluctuation around it, and $\hat s_c$ is the library
rescaled by $\hat S_j$. Both split into a technical and a biological
part:

- **Technical level.** If one capture protocol, one chemistry and one
  sequencing run serve every type, the mean technical level
  $S^{\mathrm{tech}}$ is shared, enters $c_i$, and drops out of the
  proportions. That sharing is an assumption: a type-specific capture
  (lysis, RNA content near saturation) would be confounded with
  biology.
- **Biological level.** $S^{\mathrm{bio}}_j$ is not shared:
  transcriptome size depends on the type and on its state
  [@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025;
  @fangExtrinsicBiologicalStochasticity2025]. It is what turns cell
  fractions into transcript fractions
  ([cell size](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-cell-size-covariance),
  [RNA versus cell fraction](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-uncoupling)).
- **Without spike-ins**, neither $s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c$ nor a
  type-specific capture can be separated from the biological size. The
  data identify only the product $s_c$, and only up to the constraint
  of @eq-size-factor-mean
  [@fangExtrinsicBiologicalStochasticity2025].

### What the raw covariance contains {#sec-cov-raw-decomposition}

The law of total covariance applied to @eq-cov-measurement gives

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{raw}}_j
=\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\mid j)
=\underbrace{\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j})}_{\text{Poisson sampling}}
+\underbrace{(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}})\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j}_{\text{biology}}
+\underbrace{\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}}_{\text{technical size}} .
$$ {#eq-raw-decomposition}

<!-- chk: V38a -->
It is the matrix form of
[the count covariance](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#eq-count-covariance),
grouped by what the bulk inherits. Solving for
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j$ with
$\kappa=\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}/(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}})$ gives
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{raw}}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j})-\kappa\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{raw}}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j})+\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\}$,
whose sample version, with a finite-sample correction, is
[the denoised within-type covariance](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#eq-denoised-within).
<!-- chk: V38b, V14a, V14b, V14c, V14e -->
The Poisson diagonal also attenuates every correlation of the raw
counts, most for lowly expressed genes (@sec-grn-attenuation).

### Which matrix enters the bulk {#sec-cov-bulk-inherits}

The bulk is counted once, at its own depth, from the pooled molecules.
On the reference capture scale, with $n_i$ cells drawn with proportions
$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$,

$$
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\{\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}\}
\sim\mathrm{Poisson}\Bigl(a_i\sum_{c}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}\Bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}
=\phi_i\boldsymbol{S}^{\mathrm{bio}}(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})+c_i\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}).
$$ {#eq-bulk-sampling}

Keeping each reference-counted molecule with probability $a_i\le1$
(binomial thinning) gives the same law. <!-- chk: V13a -->
A model that counts every cell at the reference depth and then
multiplies the counts by $a_i$ would scale the Poisson diagonal by
$\phi_i$ instead of $c_i$; no library preparation does that, and it is
not used. Two consequences follow. The sampling noise of the reference
does not enter the bulk; the bulk has its own, once. And the technical
size factor of the reference cells does not enter either: the bulk has
no droplets. In units of $\phi_i$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}
=\phi_i\bigl\{\boldsymbol{S}^{\mathrm{bio}}(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})
+a_i^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\bigr\},
\qquad a_i=\phi_i/c_i,
$$ {#eq-bulk-plugin}

<!-- chk: V13b -->
so, with $\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}=0$, the right plug-in depends on the bulk
depth per cell $a_i$:

- $a_i=1$, the bulk counted at the per-cell depth of the reference: the
  raw covariance is exact;
- $a_i>1$: the raw covariance over-weights the sampling diagonal by the
  factor $a_i$; the denoised covariance alone is the limit
  $a_i\to\infty$;
- $a_i<1$: the raw covariance under-weights the diagonal by the factor
  $a_i$, and the denoised one drops it;
- in every case the off-diagonal entries are those of
  $\phi_i\boldsymbol{S}^{\mathrm{bio}}$; the choice moves the gene weights
  and the correlations, not the network. Gene $g$ is dominated by
  sampling noise when $\tilde\mu_g(\boldsymbol{p})>a_iS^{\mathrm{bio}}_{gg}(\boldsymbol{p})$.

The plug-in that holds at every depth is the denoised covariance plus
the bulk sampling term $c_i\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})$.
For UMI-like bulk counts it adds no parameter, since $c_i$ and $\phi_i$
are already estimated; read counts need a dispersion $\omega_i\ge1$ in
front of the term, which one sample identifies weakly. The covariance is
then no longer proportional to $\phi_i$, so the closed form
$\hat\phi=Q/G$ of the
[closed-form scales](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#eq-sc-closed-scales)
is lost and $\phi_i$ is profiled numerically, in one dimension.

**Status.** This variant is not implemented:
[`deconvolute_single_cell()`](../reference/deconvolute_single_cell.html)
uses one matrix, and with a raw $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ it assumes
$a_i=1$ and $\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}=0$. The raw plug-in stays the default;
the denoised covariance is the target and enters as a sensitivity arm
(@tbl-cov-estimators).

**Which regime to expect.** Taking expectations of the library sizes in
@eq-bulk-sampling,

$$
a_i\approx\frac{y_{+i}}{n_i\sum_jp_{ji}S_j},
$$ {#eq-bulk-depth-per-cell}

<!-- chk: V45 -->
the bulk counts per cell over the reference counts per cell. A bulk
library is deeper in total than one droplet, but it spreads that depth
over every cell of the sample, so $a_i<1$ is the usual case. For
illustration (our numbers, not a measurement), a bulk library of
$2\times10^{7}$ counts from $10^{5}$ cells against a reference with
$5\times10^{3}$ UMIs per cell gives $a_i=0.04$; if those counts behave
as UMIs, a gene is then dominated by bulk sampling noise unless its
biological Fano factor $S^{\mathrm{bio}}_{gg}/\tilde\mu_g$ exceeds 25.
Bulk counts are reads, not molecules: amplification makes them
overdispersed ($\omega_i\ge1$), which lowers the effective depth to
$a_i/\omega_i$. The Suppinger value needs $n_i$, the number of cells
per bulk sample; it is computed in the
[reproducibility book](https://github.com/bastienchassagnol/DeCovarT_reproducibility/blob/main/docs/03-covariance-estimation.qmd).
The identities of this subsection are checked in the SymPy ledger of
the CardamomOT comparison note (`answer-cardamomOT/verification/`).

### Library normalisation without spike-ins {#sec-cov-normalisation}

The Suppinger reference has no spike-ins. Two treatments of the size
factor are possible:

| Option | Exported mean $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ | Exported covariance $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$ |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Raw per-cell counts, at most one global constant | unbiased for $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ (@eq-size-factor-mean); keeps $S_j$, so $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$ stays a cell proportion | keeps the biological size (wanted); keeps the Poisson diagonal and the technical rank-one term of @eq-raw-decomposition (unwanted; the latter inflates every correlation) |
| (b) Each cell divided by its total library | removes $S_j$: signatures become transcript fractions, and the fit returns $q_{ji}\propto p_{ji}S_j$ | removes the technical size (wanted) and the biological size (unwanted); a panel total adds closure correlations, a full-library total a smaller amount |

: Raw counts against per-cell library normalisation, without spike-ins. {#tbl-cov-normalisation}

<!-- chk: V44 -->
**Decision.** No per-cell normalisation for the exported moments. The
mean is computed on raw per-cell counts, the default signature of
[normalisation that preserves the linear mixture](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-norm-linear).
The covariance is computed on the same counts, then corrected by the
moment estimator with the share $\kappa$ bracketed:

- $\kappa=0$ treats all size variation as biological and removes only
  the Poisson diagonal;
- $\kappa=\hat\nu/(1+\hat\nu)$, with $\hat\nu$ the total extrinsic
  noise ([Fang–Pachter estimate](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-extrinsic-noise),
  the mode of the normalised covariances over gene pairs), treats it
  all as technical. It returns
  $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}$,
  approximately the covariance that option (b) estimates. <!-- chk: V14d -->

Spike-ins would reduce the bracket to one value. Ambient RNA from empty
droplets is the only possible proxy here
[TODO: check whether GSE229513 provides raw droplet matrices]{.highlight}.
Size factors remain the right tool inside the gene-wise tests of the
feature selection, where they are offsets for a nuisance
([feature selection](03-1-feature-selection.html)); that use is
different.

### One preprocessing step for every estimator {#sec-cov-preprocessing}

The denoising is a moment correction of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$, applied
before any regularisation:

1. Compute $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ and $\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j$ on the raw
   per-cell counts of the $C_j$ cells.
2. Apply [the denoised within-type covariance](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#eq-denoised-within)
   at the two ends of the bracket, $\kappa=0$ and
   $\kappa=\hat\nu/(1+\hat\nu)$.
3. Project on the positive semi-definite cone. The corrected matrix is
   indefinite in general: subtracting $\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)$
   gives negative variances to genes whose variance is close to their
   mean, and with $C_j\le G$ the null directions of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$
   become negative eigenvalues. Clipping the eigenvalues at zero is the
   nearest positive semi-definite matrix in Frobenius norm. The
   corrected covariances of errors-in-variables regression meet the
   same problem: CoCoLasso projects on the cone, Loh and Wainwright
   regularise the indefinite matrix directly
   [TODO-cite: Datta & Zou 2017, Ann. Stat. 45(6):2482–2511, doi:10.1214/16-AOS1527; Loh & Wainwright 2012, Ann. Stat. 40(3):1637–1664, doi:10.1214/12-AOS1018; not in Zotero]{.highlight}.
4. Regularise as in @tbl-cov-estimators:
   - shrinkage: target D on the denoised variances;
   - graphical lasso: the correlation of the projected matrix;
   - `SILGGM`: ranks cannot be denoised, so the support still comes
     from the nonparanormal scores; the refit under that support uses
     the projected matrix;
   - `PLNnetwork`: no correction (below).

A gene whose denoised variance is zero contributes only through the
bulk sampling term. $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j$ needs to be
positive semi-definite, not definite, once that term is in the bulk
covariance; until it is implemented, a small eigenvalue floor keeps the
plug-in invertible. The held-out score of @sec-cov-cv compares a
denoised fit with the others only after the measurement terms of
@eq-raw-decomposition are added back, because the held-out cells are
raw counts.

**`PLNnetwork` needs no moment correction, but needs a choice at
export.** Its latent covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z$ excludes the
Poisson noise by construction. Its offset, the full library $s_c$,
removes all cell-level size variation, biological size included, as
scVI's library factor does
([scVI](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-batch-methods)).
The linear-moment map decides what is put back. @eq-pln-linear-avg
without its Poisson term $\bar s\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{m})$ is
the $\kappa=0$ end; holding $s_c$ at $\bar s$ is the other end.
<!-- chk: V43 -->
The correspondence is approximate, because the offset is the observed
library, which carries Poisson noise and the variation of
$\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}$.


{{< pagebreak >}}

## Sample-size regimes {#sec-cov-regimes}

Three requirements are often conflated. They are ordered here by the
number of cells they need; the mean is estimated throughout, and
$\boldsymbol{X}_c$ is the centred $C_j\times G$ matrix of the type-$j$
cells.

### Layer 1: a regularised estimate exists ($C_j\ge2$)

DeCovarT's plug-in needs an estimate that is finite, positive definite
and unique. It does not need the zeros of
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$. The penalty, the constraint or the structure,
not the data, makes such an estimate exist when $C_j\le G$
(@tbl-cov-existence).

| Estimator | Formula | Unique positive-definite estimate when |
|---|---|---|
| Unconstrained MLE | $\boldsymbol{V}_j=\boldsymbol{X}_c^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}_c/C_j$ | $C_j\ge G+1$ and $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{X}_c=G$ |
| Linear shrinkage | $(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{V}_j+\lambda\boldsymbol{T}$, $\lambda\in(0,1]$; Ledoit–Wolf $\boldsymbol{T}=(\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{V}_j/G)\mathbf{I}$, Schäfer–Strimmer $\boldsymbol{T}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j$ | $C_j\ge2$, $\boldsymbol{T}\succ0$ and $\lambda>0$ |
| Condition-number constraint | maximum likelihood subject to $\operatorname{cond}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\le$ a bound; the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ are clipped to an interval with that ratio | $C_j\ge2$, $\boldsymbol{V}_j\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ (our reading for an estimated mean) |
| Structured $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ | factor plus diagonal, banded, or linear in known matrices | $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{V}_j=G$ in the result we read; below that, per structure |
| Graphical lasso | @eq-glasso | $C_j\ge2$, $V_{gg}>0$, $\lambda>0$, unpenalised diagonal |

: When each covariance estimator of type $j$ is well defined. {#tbl-cov-existence}

<!-- chk: V10a, V10b, V10c, V11a, V11b, V11c -->

- **Shrinkage** [@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005]
  [TODO-cite: Ledoit & Wolf 2004, J. Multivar. Anal. 88(2):365–411, doi:10.1016/S0047-259X(03)00096-4]{.highlight}:
  the smallest eigenvalue of $(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{V}_j+\lambda\boldsymbol{T}$
  is at least $\lambda$ times that of $\boldsymbol{T}$, whatever the
  rank of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$. <!-- chk: V11b -->
  The diagonal target needs every $V_{gg}>0$, hence the presence gate
  ([presence](03-1-feature-selection.html#sec-fs-presence)); the scaled
  identity needs only $\boldsymbol{V}_j\neq\boldsymbol{0}$.
- **Condition number**: Won and co-authors keep the eigenvectors of
  $\boldsymbol{V}_j$, clip its eigenvalues in closed form, and choose
  the bound by predictive likelihood; the estimate is well conditioned
  "even when $n<p$" (p. 5). Their model has a known zero mean.
  [TODO-cite: Won, Lim, Kim & Rajaratnam 2013, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 75(3):427–450, doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2012.01049.x; key in answer-cardamomOT/references.bib only]{.highlight}
- **Structure on $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$**: for linear covariance models
  the likelihood is strictly concave on
  $\{\boldsymbol{0}\prec\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\prec2\boldsymbol{V}_j\}$, but
  existence is shown for a full-rank $\boldsymbol{V}_j$, so it does not
  relax $C_j\ge G+1$; a factor model can have an unbounded likelihood
  when a specific variance tends to zero (our reading).
  [TODO-cite: Zwiernik, Uhler & Richards 2017, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 79(4):1269–1292, doi:10.1111/rssb.12217; key in answer-cardamomOT/references.bib only]{.highlight}
- **Graphical lasso**: with $\lambda>0$, positive $V_{gg}$ and an
  unpenalised diagonal, it has a unique positive definite solution for
  any $C_j\ge2$, even when $C_j<G$
  [@carterExistencePenalisedLikelihood2025].

None of these estimators needs a sparse truth. Layer 1 is all the
plug-in needs.

### Layer 2: the unconstrained maximum-likelihood estimate exists ($C_j\ge G+1$)

The rank of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ is that of $\boldsymbol{X}_c$, at most
$\min(C_j-1,G)$, with equality almost surely for Gaussian cells, since
$C_j\boldsymbol{V}_j\sim W_G(C_j-1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})$
[TODO-cite: Muirhead 1982, Aspects of Multivariate Statistical Theory, ch. 3; key in answer-cardamomOT/references.bib only]{.highlight}.
$\boldsymbol{V}_j$ is positive definite if and only if
$\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{X}_c=G$: this needs $C_j\ge G+1$ and no
exact linear relation between genes. With $C_j\le G$ the centred
profiles always satisfy one; a gene constant within the type is the
simplest, which the presence gate removes, but the gate is necessary,
not sufficient. When $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ is singular, the Gaussian
log-likelihood is unbounded above along its null directions and the
maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist. <!-- chk: V10a, V10b, V10c -->

**The precision has the same existence threshold, and a worse
accuracy.** $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j=\boldsymbol{V}_j^{-1}$
exists exactly when $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ does. Its mean, from the
inverse Wishart law, is

$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\boldsymbol{V}_j^{-1}\bigr]
=\frac{C_j}{C_j-G-2}\,\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j,
\qquad C_j\ge G+3,
$$ {#eq-inverse-wishart-bias}

<!-- chk: V40 -->
so with $C_j=2G$ the precision is inflated by a factor close to two.
The spectrum explains why: when $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}=\mathbf{I}$
and $G/C_j\to\eta<1$, the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ spread
over $[(1-\sqrt{\eta})^{2},(1+\sqrt{\eta})^{2}]$
(Marchenko–Pastur), and the smallest ones drive
$\boldsymbol{V}_j^{-1}$.
[TODO-cite: Marchenko & Pastur 1967, Math. USSR Sb. 1(4):457–483, doi:10.1070/SM1967v001n04ABEH001994]{.highlight}
A consistent estimate of a dense $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ in operator
norm needs $G/C_j\to0$, that is $C_j\gg G$, not only $C_j>G$.

**Between layers 1 and 2: the MLE on a fixed graph.** Dempster's refit
under the zeros of a graph $\mathcal{G}$ with edge set $E$,

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{E}
=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succ0}
\log\det\boldsymbol{\Omega}-\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{V}_j\boldsymbol{\Omega})
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\omega_{gg'}=0\ \ \forall\,(g,g')\notin E,
$$ {#eq-hard-cov-selection}

exists for almost every sample once $C_j-1\ge\operatorname{mlt}(\mathcal{G})$,
the maximum-likelihood threshold of the graph (with an estimated mean;
the published statements assume a known zero mean). On that graph:

- a *clique* is a set of genes pairwise joined by edges, and
  $\operatorname{cl}(\mathcal{G})$ the size of the largest;
- a graph is *chordal* if every cycle through four or more genes has a
  chord; $\operatorname{tw}(\mathcal{G})+1$ is the smallest clique number
  of a chordal graph containing $\mathcal{G}$;
- $\operatorname{cl}(\mathcal{G})\le\operatorname{mlt}(\mathcal{G})\le\operatorname{tw}(\mathcal{G})+1\le G$,
  with equality on the left for chordal graphs, and the smallest $k$
  with an empty $k$-core also bounds $\operatorname{mlt}$ from above, so
  sparse graphs have small thresholds
  [TODO-cite: Uhler 2012, Ann. Stat. 40(1):238–261, doi:10.1214/11-AOS957; Gross & Sullivant 2018, Bernoulli 24(1):386–407, doi:10.3150/16-BEJ881; Bernstein & Outlaw 2023, arXiv:2312.03145; keys in answer-cardamomOT/references.bib only]{.highlight}.

Bernstein and Outlaw simulate graphs selected by the graphical lasso
from independent Gaussian data ($G\le9$): the probability that the
selected graph has $\operatorname{mlt}\le C_j$ rises with $\lambda$ and
with $C_j$; with one observation the graphical lasso never returned
the empty graph, the only graph whose estimate then exists (pp. 4–5).
This intermediate threshold governs the refit of `SILGGM`
(@sec-cov-npn).

### Layer 3: the support is recovered

Support recovery by the graphical lasso needs
$C_j\gtrsim d^{2}\log G$, an irrepresentability condition, bounded
eigenvalues and a minimum $|\omega_{gg'}|$
[TODO-cite: Ravikumar, Wainwright, Raskutti & Yu 2011, Electron. J. Stat. 5:935–980, doi:10.1214/11-EJS631]{.highlight}.
Neighbourhood selection needs $d\log G$
[@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 41], under its own
neighbourhood stability condition
[TODO-cite: Meinshausen & Bühlmann 2006, Ann. Stat. 34(3):1436–1462, doi:10.1214/009053606000000281]{.highlight}.
These are orders without constants. With $G=1{,}417$ and $d=10$,
$d^{2}\log G\approx726$ and $d\log G\approx73$ (natural logarithm);
hubs raise $d$. <!-- chk: V42 -->
For a sparse graph, $d^{2}\log G<G$ and the threshold lies between
layers 1 and 2: far above two cells, below the
$G+1$ that the unconstrained estimate needs. For a dense graph,
$d$ is of order $G$ and the threshold exceeds layer 2. On models derived
from gene expression the irrepresentability conditions never held
[@heinävaaraInconsistencyℓ1penalisedSparse2016], and they involve the
unknown $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$: "we can never verify them on real
data" [@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 77].

**Consequence for DeCovarT.** The plug-in needs layer 1 only. The
refit of `SILGGM` needs the intermediate threshold of layer 2. Any
biological reading of the zeros needs layer 3, which is out of scope
here; it can be probed by simulating precisions at the observed $C_j$
with `simulate_hierarchical_grn_moments()` and measuring recovery. The
reproducibility book tabulates the three thresholds for the eleven
Suppinger units.


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Covariance estimator {#sec-cov-estimators}

## Schäfer and Strimmer's linear shrinkage {#sec-cov-shrinkage}

Schäfer and Strimmer shrink the sample covariance towards a target
$\boldsymbol{T}$, $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\lambda\boldsymbol{T}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{V}_j$
[@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005, eq. 3]. Their target D
("diagonal, unequal variance") keeps the variances and shrinks the
correlations towards zero (Table 1, eq. 10):

$$
\hat\Sigma_{gg}=V_{gg},
\qquad
\hat\Sigma_{gg'}=(1-\lambda)\,R_{j,gg'}\sqrt{V_{gg}V_{g'g'}},
\qquad
\hat\lambda^{\ast}
=\frac{\sum_{g\neq g'}\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(R_{j,gg'})}
      {\sum_{g\neq g'}R_{j,gg'}^{2}},
$$ {#eq-shrink-target-d}

with $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ truncated to $[0,1]$. The closed form
minimises the Frobenius risk (the Ledoit–Wolf lemma). The estimate is
positive definite for any $C_j$ and $G$ once every $V_{gg}>0$, invariant
to the scale of each gene, and costs about two sample covariances. Its
precision is dense; partial correlations and a local-FDR graph can be
read from it if wanted (eqs. 11–15).

The Frobenius risk is not the Gaussian likelihood that DeCovarT
evaluates. $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ is therefore only the starting point of
the cross-validated search of @sec-cov-cv. In `corpcor::cov.shrink()`,
`lambda.var = 0` reproduces target D; the default also shrinks the
variances towards their median. The plug-in uses raw per-cell counts
(@sec-cov-normalisation); the denoised arm applies the same target to
the projected denoised matrix (@sec-cov-preprocessing).

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Sparse precision estimators: sensitivity analyses {#sec-cov-sparse}

The three estimators below test the plug-in against the assumption that
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ is sparse. Each exports a covariance on the
linear scale, so all are scored by the same criterion (@sec-cov-cv).

## Graphical lasso with an unpenalised diagonal {#sec-cov-glasso}

On the correlation $\boldsymbol{R}_j$, with
$\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{V}_j)$,

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}
=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succ0}
\Bigl[-\log\det\boldsymbol{\Omega}
+\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{R}_j\boldsymbol{\Omega})
+\lambda\sum_{g\neq g'}|\omega_{gg'}|\Bigr],
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{-1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{-1/2}
$$ {#eq-glasso}

[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008; @mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011].
Working on $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ puts every gene on one scale for one
$\lambda$; rescaling leaves the zeros and the partial correlations
unchanged. With the diagonal unpenalised, the fitted covariance
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{R}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}^{-1}$
has unit diagonal, so the exported
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{R}\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j^{1/2}$
keeps the sample variances exactly. On the selected edges,
$\hat\Sigma_{R,gg'}=R_{j,gg'}+\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\hat\omega_{gg'})$
in the sign convention of @eq-glasso; off them,
$|\hat\Sigma_{R,gg'}-R_{j,gg'}|\le\lambda$.

**Why `glasso` rather than `huge`:** `huge.glasso()` always penalises the
diagonal, which inflates every variance by $\lambda$ (@sec-cov-diagonal),
whereas `glasso::glasso(penalize.diagonal = FALSE)` leaves it free
[@zhaoHugePackageHighdimensional]. `glasso` 1.11 penalises the diagonal
by default, so the argument must be set.

## `SILGGM` after the nonparanormal map {#sec-cov-npn}

`SILGGM` tests the entries of a Gaussian precision with a global FDR
guarantee [@zhangSILGGMExtensivePackage2018]. Its input must be close to
Gaussian, so the counts are first mapped to nonparanormal scores.

**The map.** A nonparanormal vector has monotone $f_g$ with
$f_g(x_g)\sim\mathcal{N}$ jointly
[@liuNonparanormalSemiparametricEstimation2009]. By Sklar's theorem
(appendix, @sec-cov-perspectives) the latent Gaussian copula carries
the graph; the margins carry the scale. With $r_{cg}$ the rank of
$x_{gc}$ among the $C_j$ cells, two regularisations keep $\Phi^{-1}$
finite:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{shrinkage:}&\quad \tilde z_{gc}=\Phi^{-1}\!\Bigl(\frac{r_{cg}}{C_j+1}\Bigr),\\
\text{truncation:}&\quad \tilde z_{gc}=\Phi^{-1}\!\Bigl[\min\bigl\{1-\delta_{C_j},\max(\delta_{C_j},r_{cg}/C_j)\bigr\}\Bigr],
\qquad
\delta_{n}=\frac{1}{4n^{1/4}\sqrt{\pi\log n}} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-npn-shrink-trunc}

Shrinkage is preferred. It moves each probability by at most
$1/(C_j+1)$ and keeps every rank distinct. Truncation gives all ranks
beyond $\delta_{C_j}$ the same score; $\delta_{C_j}$ is of order
$C_j^{-1/4}$, fixed by the sample size rather than by the data, so it
clips exactly the heavy upper tails that single-cell profiles have.
Neither map helps with ties: all the zeros of a sparse gene share one
score, so a gene detected in few cells carries few distinct values
(@sec-cov-diagonal, cause (ii)).

**De-sparsified edges and the FDR support.** The graphical-lasso
estimate $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ of the scores is biased by the
$\ell_1$ term: its KKT condition reads
$\boldsymbol{R}_j^{\mathrm{npn}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^{-1}+\lambda\widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}}=\boldsymbol{0}$,
with $\boldsymbol{R}_j^{\mathrm{npn}}$ the correlation of the scores and
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}}$ a subgradient of the $\ell_1$ norm. One
Newton step on the unpenalised score removes that bias,

$$
\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
=2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\boldsymbol{R}_j^{\mathrm{npn}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}+\lambda\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}},
$$ {#eq-desparsify}

and $\sqrt{C_j}(\check\omega_{gg'}-\omega_{gg'})$ is asymptotically
$\mathcal{N}(0,\omega_{gg}\omega_{g'g'}+\omega_{gg'}^{2})$ under
sparsity and rate conditions
[@jankovaConfidenceIntervalsHighdimensional2015]. `SILGGM`
(`D-S_GL`, `global = TRUE`) thresholds the resulting $z$-statistics by
the global FDR rule of @liuGaussianGraphicalModel2013.
$\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is dense and is not exported. Its role is
the support.

**What DeCovarT receives.** The covariance on the linear scale is refit
under the zeros of the support (@eq-hard-cov-selection), on
$\boldsymbol{V}_j$ or on the projected denoised matrix
(@sec-cov-preprocessing). Two caveats follow. The refit exists only for
$C_j-1\ge\operatorname{mlt}$ of the support (@sec-cov-regimes, layer 2);
below it a penalty is needed again and the arm loses its advantage over
@sec-cov-glasso. And a zero partial correlation of the latent copula
need not be a zero partial correlation of the linear counts, so
imposing the support on the linear scale is an approximation. The
held-out score of @sec-cov-cv measures what that approximation costs.
The tuning parameter is the FDR level $\alpha$.

## Poisson–lognormal network {#sec-cov-pln}

`PLNnetwork` separates the Poisson sampling layer from the latent
covariance [@chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018;
@chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021] (@fig-grn-pln):

$$
\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}_z,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z),
\qquad
x_{gc}\mid\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}\sim\mathcal{P}\bigl(s_c\,e^{z_{gc}}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-pln}

with an $\ell_1$ penalty on the off-diagonal entries of
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_z=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z^{-1}$ (diagonal
unpenalised). The offset $\log s_c$ is the library size of cell $c$
over all genes. A sum over the panel would depend on the panel genes
and absorb part of the type signal. The offset fixes the coefficient of
$\log s_c$ at one, so $\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}$ describes expression
per unit of sequencing exposure. One model is fitted per type (and
time); a single model with type dummies would share one
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z$ across types.

The likelihood integrates $\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}$ and has no closed
form. Variational EM maximises the evidence lower bound,
$\log p(\boldsymbol{x})-\operatorname{KL}\{q\,\|\,p(\boldsymbol{z}\mid\boldsymbol{x})\}$,
over a Gaussian family $q$; the KL gap is zero only if $q$ is the
true posterior. The closed-form updates of $q$ replace a Monte Carlo
E-step, which is what makes the fit practical at single-cell sizes
[@chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018].

**Comparison on the linear scale.** The latent covariance is not
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$. With
$\boldsymbol{m}=\exp\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_z+\tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z)\}$
(elementwise), the log-normal and Poisson moments give, for one cell,

$$
\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\mid s_c)=s_c\boldsymbol{m},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\mid s_c)
=s_c\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{m})
+s_c^{2}\,(\boldsymbol{m}\boldsymbol{m}^{\top})\circ\bigl(e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z}-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-pln-linear}

<!-- chk: V3 -->
and, averaged over the size factors of the scored cells, with
$\bar s$ and $\overline{s^{2}}$ their first two moments,

$$
\mathbb{E}\boldsymbol{x}=\bar s\,\boldsymbol{m},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}
=\bar s\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{m})
+(\boldsymbol{m}\boldsymbol{m}^{\top})\circ\bigl(\overline{s^{2}}\,e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z}-\bar s^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-pln-linear-avg}

<!-- chk: V3 -->
The variance of $s_c$ adds the rank-one term
$\operatorname{Var}(s)\,\boldsymbol{m}\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}$: depth
variation correlates every pair of genes. Which part of it, and whether
the Poisson term, is exported is the bracket of
@sec-cov-preprocessing. These moments are what the PLN arm exports and
what @sec-cov-cv scores; the scale must match the one used for the
mean signature.

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-grn-pln

The latent log-expression $\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}$ carries the covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}$ and its precision; the counts add independent Poisson noise given $\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}$ and the size factor $s_c$. Covariances between genes come only from $\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}$ (and from the spread of $s_c$); the Poisson term adds to the diagonal only.
