# Hyper-parameter tuning {#sec-cov-tuning}

## Cross-validation of the Gaussian log-score {#sec-cov-cv}

Each estimator of @tbl-cov-estimators has one tuned parameter:
$\lambda$ for both shrinkages (searched around $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$),
$\lambda$ for the graphical lasso, $\alpha$ for `SILGGM`, $\lambda$ for
`PLNnetwork`. All five are tuned by the same score.

**Score.** Split the $C_j$ cells of type $j$ into $K$ folds. Fit
$(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)})$
on the other folds, exported on the linear scale, and score the
$C_{j,k}$ held-out cells by their mean Gaussian log-density,

$$
\ell^{(k)}
=-\frac12\Bigl[\log\det\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)}
+\operatorname{tr}\bigl\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)})^{-1}\boldsymbol{V}_{j,k}\bigr\}
+G\log2\pi\Bigr],
$$ {#eq-heldout-loglik}

with
$\boldsymbol{V}_{j,k}=C_{j,k}^{-1}\sum_{c\in k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)})(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)})^{\top}$.
The tuning value maximises $K^{-1}\sum_k\ell^{(k)}$ (or the one
standard-error rule). Minus the cross-validated score estimates the
Kullback–Leibler risk of the fitted law up to a constant
[@commengesDynamicalBiostatisticalModels2015, § 2.4.2]. It applies to
maximum-likelihood, penalised and shrinkage fits alike, whereas AIC
and BIC are justified for the maximum-likelihood estimate. The folds
split cells of one specimen. The score therefore measures prediction
of new cells of that specimen, which is the population of
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$, and says nothing about new specimens
[@zimmermanPracticalSolutionPseudoreplication2021].

**Scoring a denoised fit.** The held-out cells are raw counts, so a
denoised fit is scored after the measurement terms of
@eq-raw-decomposition are added back:
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j+\operatorname{diag}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j})+\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa}\bigl(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_j+\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\bigr)$.
<!-- chk: V38c -->
The comparison then measures only how the biological part is
regularised. Cross-validation cannot choose $\kappa$, because every
$\kappa$ reconstructs the same raw moments up to regularisation;
$\kappa$ stays a bracket.

::: {#prp-gaussian-logscore}
## The Gaussian log-score is proper for the mean and the covariance

For a test cell with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast}$ and covariance
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast}$, whatever its law,

$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl\{-\log\phi_G(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\bigr\}
=\tfrac12\bigl\{\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
+\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})
+(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast})
+G\log2\pi\bigr\}.
$$ {#eq-stein-score}

It is minimised over $(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, uniquely,
at $(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Only the first two moments of $\boldsymbol{x}$ enter, because the
log-density is quadratic in $\boldsymbol{x}$. At
$\boldsymbol{\mu}=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast}$ the excess over the value at
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast}$ is half of Stein's loss,
$\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})-\log\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast})-G=\sum_k(\ell_k-\log\ell_k-1)\ge0$,
with $\ell_k$ the eigenvalues of
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast}$; it is zero only
when every $\ell_k=1$, that is
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\ast}$. The mean term is a
non-negative quadratic form, zero only at
$\boldsymbol{\mu}=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\ast}$.
<!-- chk: V2 -->
:::

@prp-gaussian-logscore is what DeCovarT's bulk likelihood needs: the
bulk law is Gaussian by the central limit theorem over many cells, not
because single cells are Gaussian, and it uses only the mean and the
covariance.

**Comparing estimators: nested cross-validation.** Tuning needs one
loop. Comparing the five tuned estimators needs two: an inner loop that
chooses each tuning parameter on the training part of an outer fold,
and an outer loop that scores the tuned estimators on cells the tuning
never saw. Reporting the inner-loop maximum as the estimator's
performance is optimistic, because it is the maximum over a grid.
Compare estimators by their paired outer-fold differences, with the
diagonal covariance $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_j$ as the baseline.

::: {#thm-uacv}
## Universal approximate cross-validation

Let $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ solve an estimating equation with mean
estimating function $\Phi$, and let $\Psi$ be a mean assessment loss
(here minus the log-score of @eq-heldout-loglik). Then the
leave-one-out loss is approximated from the single fit by

$$
\mathrm{UACV}=\Psi(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\boldsymbol{H}_{\Phi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-uacv}

where $\boldsymbol{H}_{\Phi}$ is the Hessian of the estimating
function and $\boldsymbol{U}$ (their $\boldsymbol{K}$) the mean
cross-product of the per-cell assessment and estimating scores; the
error is $O_p(C_j^{-2})$. For a maximum-likelihood fit assessed by its
own log-likelihood, UACV is the Takeuchi information criterion divided
by $2C_j$, and a smooth penalty enters $\boldsymbol{H}_{\Phi}$ and
lowers the correction (Commenges et al. 2012, eqs. 6–7, pp. 7–8).
[TODO-cite: Commenges, Proust-Lima, Samieri & Liquet 2012, arXiv:1206.1753]{.highlight}
:::

An $\ell_1$ penalty is not differentiable at zero. For the graphical
lasso and `PLNnetwork` we apply @eq-uacv on the active set, with the
support held fixed; that restriction is our reading, not the paper's.

## Other criteria and diagnostics {#sec-cov-other-criteria}

The cross-validated score selects. The diagnostics below describe a
selected fit; they need no true graph.

::: {#nte-cov-criteria .callout-note collapse="true" title="Diagnostics for regularised covariances and sparse precisions"}

Each diagnostic in the table is computed on the exported
$(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j)$
on the linear scale. It needs neither an edge set nor a count of
degrees of freedom, so it applies to the shrinkage plug-in and to the
three sparse arms alike.

| Diagnostic | Question it answers | Computation |
|---|---|---|
| Held-out log-score; TIC and UACV (@thm-uacv) | Does the fit predict new cells of the specimen? | @eq-heldout-loglik on outer folds; @eq-uacv from one fit |
| Condition number and spectrum | How far does the regulariser move the extreme eigenvalues? | eigenvalues of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$ against the Marchenko–Pastur band of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ (@eq-inverse-wishart-bias) |
| Technical stability | Is the estimate reproducible within this specimen? | within-type cell bootstrap, labels fixed: Frobenius and Bures spread of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j$, spread of the selected tuning value |
| Separation of types | Can DeCovarT tell two types apart? | Kullback–Leibler, Jeffreys, Hellinger and `MixSim` overlap between the exported Gaussians [@melnykovMixSimPackageSimulating2012; @R-MixSim]; Bures–Wasserstein ([two-scale transport](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-bisque-ot)) |

: Diagnostics that apply to every estimator of @tbl-cov-estimators. {#tbl-cov-diagnostics}

For two non-degenerate Gaussians
$P_j=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)$,

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{j}\parallel P_{\ell})
=\tfrac12\Bigl[
\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})
+(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})
-G
+\ln\frac{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}}{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}}
\Bigr],
$$ {#eq-kl-gauss}

and Jeffreys' divergence is its symmetrisation. The bootstrap interval
is conditional on this atlas: a biological (multi-organoid) bootstrap
is unavailable, and reporting a cell bootstrap as between-specimen
uncertainty is pseudoreplication
([reproducibility book, pseudoreplication](https://github.com/bastienchassagnol/DeCovarT_reproducibility/blob/main/docs/02-feature-selection.qmd)).

**Criteria that need a sparse support.** EBIC and BIC count $|E|+G$
parameters, so they rank sparse maximum-likelihood fits but not
shrinkage intensities, and at small $C_j$ EBIC returns empty graphs
(@sec-grn-screening) [@foygelExtendedBayesianInformation2010]. StARS
chooses the least regularised graph whose edge instability across
subsamples stays below a threshold
[@liuStabilityApproachRegularization2010]. Stability selection reports
edge-inclusion frequencies under subsampling
[@meinshausenStabilitySelection2010]. Thresholded adaptive validation
targets the support as well
[@laszkiewiczThresholdedAdaptiveValidation2021]. These are reported
for the sparse arms only, beside the cross-validated choice.

:::


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Discussion and conclusions {#sec-cov-discussion}

## The diagonal of the precision and near-diagonal estimates {#sec-cov-diagonal}

### A diagonal entry is a conditional variance

In a Gaussian graphical model,
$\omega_{gg}=1/\operatorname{Var}(x_g\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{-g})$: the
part of gene $g$'s variance that the other panel genes do not explain.
On counts it mixes transcriptional bursting and auto-regulation,
regulators outside the panel, and Poisson sampling, and
$\boldsymbol{V}_j$ alone cannot separate them; at droplet depths
sampling is the largest share for most genes
[@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021]. By @eq-schur-update,
$\omega_{gg}$ also changes when a neighbour of $g$ enters or leaves the
panel. A diagonal entry is neither a self-loop nor its sign
(@nte-cov-lyapunov).

### Penalising the diagonal biases the variances

With a penalised diagonal the KKT conditions give
$\hat\Sigma_{gg}=V_{gg}+\lambda$
[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008; @mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011].
On the correlation scale every implied correlation shrinks by about
$1/(1+\lambda)$, in the same direction as Poisson attenuation
(@sec-grn-attenuation). The penalty does not move the empty-graph
threshold of @sec-grn-screening. DeCovarT's likelihood uses the
variances directly, so this bias enters the deconvolution.

::: callout-important
## Decision

Never penalise the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$: `glasso` with
`penalize.diagonal = FALSE`, `PLNnetwork` with an unpenalised diagonal,
shrinkage target D with `lambda.var = 0`. Schemes that re-estimate the
diagonal after the off-diagonal step are compatible with this rule:
SPACE estimates conditional variances from residuals
[@pengPartialCorrelationEstimation2009]; the partial-correlation
graphical lasso penalises only the partial correlations and is scale
invariant, computed by alternating the two blocks
[@carterExistenceOptimisationPartial2025]; the simplest version is a
refit without penalty on a selected support (@eq-hard-cov-selection).
:::

### Why near-diagonal precisions appear {#sec-grn-diagonal}

On Suppinger, an earlier pipeline (`huge`, EBIC) returned mostly
diagonal $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j$. Five causes compete with
"no dependence"; the first three are checkable.

- **(i) Pipeline fallbacks.** A gene constant within a type made the
  earlier script return a diagonal covariance for the whole type;
  failed solves were replaced by a diagonal that EBIC could select; and
  EBIC mixed a correlation-scale fit with a covariance-scale
  likelihood. These are fixed in the reproducibility code, and the
  presence gate of the feature selection
  ([presence](03-1-feature-selection.html#sec-fs-presence)) prevents the
  first upstream.
- **(ii) A transformation that ignores the count law.** Rank scores give
  all zeros of a sparse gene one tied value, and standardising by the
  marginal variance treats a Poisson-dominated gene and an
  overdispersed gene alike. Both flatten correlations before any
  penalty acts (Wu et al. 2020 warn against a naive nonparanormal map
  on counts). [TODO-cite: Wu et al. 2020, joint Gaussian copula graphical models (JGCGM); key wuJointLearningMultiple2020 is in the book bib only]{.highlight}
- **(iii) A panel built against within-type covariance.** Genes chosen for
  a large between- to within-type ratio have small within-type
  variance, where sampling noise dominates. Such a panel removes the
  covariance DeCovarT is meant to model
  ([selection effect](03-1-feature-selection.html#sec-fs-selection-effect)).
  If the discriminative genes are close to conditionally independent
  within each type, the covariance adds little to the mean signature,
  which is itself a result.
- **(iv) A detection threshold** (@sec-grn-screening).
- **(v) Poisson attenuation** (@sec-grn-attenuation), which the
  denoised covariance of @sec-raw-vs-denoised undoes in expectation.

### A screening threshold, not an estimated absence {#sec-grn-screening}

For any $\lambda$, the graphical lasso on $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ returns a
diagonal $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ exactly when
$\max_{g\neq g'}|R_{j,gg'}|\le\lambda$, with or without a penalised
diagonal [@mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011]: "A large enough penalty
level produces an empty graph"
[@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 39]. Two orders of
magnitude make that likely on single-cell data.

- **Noise level.** Under independence the largest of the $G(G-1)/2$
  sample correlations is about $\sqrt{4\log G/C_j}$, that is $0.35$ for
  $G=500$ and $C_j=200$. A penalty that controls false edges sits near
  that level.
- **EBIC cost per edge.** With $\gamma=0.5$, EBIC charges
  $\log C_j+4\gamma\log G\approx17.7$ per edge at the same sizes. One
  edge of partial correlation $\rho$ raises twice the log-likelihood by
  about $C_j\rho^{2}$, so only $|\rho|\gtrsim0.30$ survives.

Neighbourhood selection behaves the same way: its finite-sample penalty
sets every coefficient to zero when all
$|r_{gg'}|\le\tilde\Phi^{-1}\{\alpha/(2G^{2})\}/\sqrt{C_j}$, about $0.55$
for $G=1000$, $C_j=100$ and $\alpha=0.05$ (Meinshausen & Bühlmann 2006,
eq. 9), and partial correlations below order $C_j^{-(1-\xi)/2}$ are not
detected (assumption 5). A diagonal estimate says that no partial
correlation is large **relative to $\sqrt{\log G/C_j}$**, not that the
partial correlations are zero. The covariance plug-in avoids the
threshold: shrinkage keeps every correlation, damped by $1-\lambda$.

### Measurement attenuation on counts {#sec-grn-attenuation}

On UMI counts the observed covariance is the latent covariance plus a
diagonal sampling term (@eq-raw-decomposition, @eq-pln-linear). Every
correlation is attenuated, most for lowly expressed genes
[@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021;
@chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021], which pushes
$\max|R_{j,gg'}|$ under the threshold of @sec-grn-screening. For two
genes with latent log-scale correlation $0.6$, latent variances $1$ and
$e^{\mu_z}=0.5$ at $s_c=1$, @eq-pln-linear gives a mean count of $0.82$
and a raw linear-scale correlation of about $0.28$. Removing the
Poisson diagonal (@sec-cov-preprocessing, $\kappa=0$) raises it to
$(e^{0.6}-1)/(e-1)\approx0.48$, the correlation of the log-normal
expression itself; the remaining gap to $0.6$ is the log-to-linear map,
not noise. <!-- chk: V3, V41 -->
The chunk below checks these values by simulation.

```{r attenuation}
#| eval: false
set.seed(20261015)
n_cells <- 5000
latent_cor <- 0.6
z <- MASS::mvrnorm(
  n_cells,
  mu = rep(log(0.5), 2),
  Sigma = matrix(c(1, latent_cor, latent_cor, 1), 2)
)
x <- matrix(stats::rpois(length(z), exp(z)), ncol = 2)
m <- exp(log(0.5) + 0.5)
pln_cor <- m^2 * (exp(latent_cor) - 1) / (m + m^2 * (exp(1) - 1))
v <- stats::cov(x)
v_denoised <- v - diag(colMeans(x))
round(
  c(
    latent = stats::cor(z)[1, 2],
    linear_counts = stats::cor(x)[1, 2],
    pln_moment_map = pln_cor,
    denoised = v_denoised[1, 2] / sqrt(prod(diag(v_denoised))),
    denoised_theory = (exp(latent_cor) - 1) / (exp(1) - 1),
    mean_count = mean(x)
  ),
  2
)
```

::: {#nte-cov-lyapunov .callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-regulation belongs to directed dynamic models"}

CardamomOT estimates a directed self-interaction $\theta_{ii}$ for each
gene and gives it no specific penalty beyond its common $\ell_1$ term
towards a prior network; a positive auto-activation with a negative
basal term is "the most parsimonious way to produce bistability for an
isolated gene" (Maugé & Ventre 2026, p. 28, citing Ferrell 2002).
[TODO-cite: Maugé & Ventre 2026, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014838]{.highlight}
[TODO-cite: Ferrell 2002, doi:10.1016/S0955-0674(02)00314-9 (journal line on p. 1 disagrees with the DOI; verify on Crossref)]{.highlight}
Such a parameter is linked to a precision only through the stationary
covariance of a linearised model. For
$\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}$
with noise covariance $\boldsymbol{Q}$, the stationary covariance
solves the Lyapunov equation
$\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{Q}=\boldsymbol{0}$.
For two genes with self-loops $-\tau_1,-\tau_2$, an edge $1\to2$ of
weight $k$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2)$, writing
$\chi=(\tau_1+\tau_2)^{2}q_2+k^{2}q_1$,

$$
\omega_{11}=\frac{2(\tau_1+\tau_2)\{\tau_1(\tau_1+\tau_2)q_2+k^{2}q_1\}}{q_1\,\chi},
\qquad
\omega_{22}=\frac{2\tau_2(\tau_1+\tau_2)^{2}}{\chi},
\qquad
\omega_{12}=-\frac{2\tau_2(\tau_1+\tau_2)k}{\chi}.
$$ {#eq-lyapunov-two-gene}

<!-- chk: V5 -->
Each diagonal entry depends on both self-loops, the edge and both noise
levels; only for $k=0$ does it reduce to $2\tau_g/q_g$, which still
mixes the self-loop with the noise. For a three-gene chain
$1\to2\to3$ the stationary $\omega_{13}$ is non-zero for generic
parameters although genes 1 and 3 share no edge.
<!-- chk: V5 (three-gene chain) -->
A GGM diagonal is therefore neither a self-loop nor its sign. Strong
positive self-loops also produce bistable, hence bimodal, within-type
laws, which a Gaussian $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ cannot represent; the
DeCovarT counterpart is to split the type into subtypes.

:::


# References

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Perspectives {#sec-cov-perspectives .appendix}

## Other techniques to infer undirected networks {.unnumbered .appendix}

- **Copulas with GAMLSS margins.** `scDesign3` fits each gene by a
  generalised additive model for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS),
  for example a negative binomial whose mean and dispersion depend on
  the type with the library size as offset, and joins the genes by a
  copula [@songScDesign3GeneratesRealistic2024]. A GAMLSS relaxes the
  exponential family and models every distribution parameter, but
  assumes independent observations (Stasinopoulos & Rigby 2007, p. 2),
  so dependence needs the copula.
  [TODO-cite: Stasinopoulos & Rigby 2007, J. Stat. Softw. 23(7); DOI not printed in the PDF, take it from JSS/Zotero]{.highlight}
  By Sklar's theorem
  $F(\boldsymbol{x})=C\{F_1(x_1),\ldots,F_G(x_G)\}$, with $C$ unique
  when the margins are continuous; for counts it is unique only on the
  ranges of the margins, so `scDesign2`/`scDesign3` randomise the
  quantile, $u_{gc}=(1-v_{gc})F_{gc}(x_{gc}-1)+v_{gc}F_{gc}(x_{gc})$
  with $v_{gc}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)$ (Sun et al. 2021).
  [TODO-cite: Sun et al. 2021, scDesign2, doi:10.1186/s13059-021-02367-2]{.highlight}
  The likelihood splits into a marginal and a copula part, so the two
  can be selected separately. The copula correlation is not
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$: linear-scale moments of a copula model
  need Monte Carlo or a moment map like @eq-pln-linear. The empirical
  Gaussian copula is singular when $C_j<G$; a sparse precision or a vine
  copula is then needed. Appendix S5 uses this model as a calibration
  simulator ([S5, simulator](S5-misspecification.html#sec-s5-simulator)).
- **Factor and sparse-plus-low-rank models.** A few unmeasured
  programmes make the marginal precision dense. Writing
  $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{marg}}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{sparse}}-\boldsymbol{L}$,
  $\boldsymbol{L}\succeq0$ of low rank (Chandrasekaran et al. 2012),
  [TODO-cite: Chandrasekaran, Parrilo & Willsky 2012, doi:10.1214/11-AOS949]{.highlight}
  or a factor-plus-diagonal covariance, gives a dense plug-in with few
  parameters. Depth variation is one such rank-one factor
  (@eq-pln-linear-avg).
- **Other estimators of the same Gaussian graph.** Neighbourhood
  selection regresses each gene on the others, $\theta^{g}_{g'}=-\omega_{gg'}/\omega_{gg}$,
  and combines neighbourhoods by an AND or an OR rule; it is parallel,
  needs $d\log G$ cells, but gives a support, not a precision. SPACE
  makes the regressions joint and recovers hubs better
  [@pengPartialCorrelationEstimation2009]. CLIME needs no
  irrepresentability condition [@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015,
  p. 42]. The D-trace loss
  $\tfrac12\langle\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{2},\boldsymbol{V}_j\rangle-\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{\Omega}$
  has a weaker irrepresentability condition than the graphical lasso
  in Zhang and Zou's AR examples [@zhangSparsePrecisionMatrix2014]. A
  graphical horseshoe replaces the penalty path by global–local
  shrinkage [@liGraphicalHorseshoeEstimator2019]. These change the bias
  and the assumptions, not the detection limit of @sec-grn-screening.
- **Matrix-variate models.** `GmGM` models dependence between genes and
  between cells through a Kronecker sum of two precisions; the sum
  cannot separate regulation inside a cell from dependence across cells
  (Andrew et al. 2026).
  [TODO-cite: Andrew et al. 2026, GmGM; key andrewMakingMultiaxisGaussian2026 is in the book bib only]{.highlight}
- **Algorithm unrolling.** Iterative sparse-precision solvers become
  trainable layers ([Monga et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1109/MSP.2020.3016905);
  [GLAD](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00271)); PLN-Tree adds a tree of
  modules to the PLN
  ([Chaussard et al. 2024](https://hal.science/hal-04622671v1)).

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {#nte-cov-joint .callout-note title="Joint and shared-topology estimation across types"}

Rare types have few cells, and estimating each covariance alone wastes
the structure they share with abundant types. A topology shared across
types and refined per type is the natural scheme. The families differ
in what they share.

- **Shrunk covariances.** The intertwined lasso fits each type on
  $\alpha\boldsymbol{V}_j+(1-\alpha)\bar{\boldsymbol{V}}$, with
  $\bar{\boldsymbol{V}}$ the cell-weighted pooled covariance
  [@chiquetInferringMultipleGraphical2011;
  @chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, pp. 49–50].
- **Shared support, free weights.** The group graphical lasso
  [@danaherJointGraphicalLasso2012] and the cooperative lasso
  [@chiquetInferringMultipleGraphical2011;
  @chiquetSparsitySigncoherentGroups2012] share edges across types. The
  cooperative lasso assumes **sign coherence**: an edge may change
  magnitude but not sign between types, because "sign swaps are very
  unlikely" [@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 51].
- **Shared weights.** The fused graphical lasso penalises
  $|\omega^{(j)}_{gg'}-\omega^{(\ell)}_{gg'}|$
  [@danaherJointGraphicalLasso2012]; PLNFGL puts a Poisson–lognormal
  layer under it [@zhaiPLNFGLJointEstimation2026].
- **Block priors.** SIMoNe penalises edges within modules less than
  edges between modules, with modules from a stochastic block model
  learnt by variational EM
  ([Chiquet et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btn637);
  @hollandStochasticBlockmodelsFirst1983).
- **The difference itself.** A D-trace loss on
  $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_1-\boldsymbol{\Omega}_2$ estimates the rewiring
  without either network, and only the difference must be sparse
  [@yuanDifferentialNetworkAnalysis2017;
  @plaksienkoMethodsDifferentialNetwork2025].

---

**Sign-coherent penalties are preferred.** The joint graphical lasso
weights each type's log-likelihood by its cell count $C_j$, and the
intertwined lasso pools covariances with the same weights. With one
dominant population, a shared or fused penalty then lets the abundant
type erase edges that only the rare types carry, and pulls the
rare-type weights towards the dominant network. The argument concerns
losses weighted by $C_j$; the single-precision D-trace loss of
@zhangSparsePrecisionMatrix2014 has no such weighting, and its
differential extension targets the difference rather than a shared
network. DeCovarT also separates
types partly through their covariance differences, which fusion
shrinks. A shared support with sign coherence keeps the magnitudes
free. Whatever the penalty, check by the nested score of @sec-cov-cv,
per type, that the rare types do not lose held-out likelihood. Separate
fits, as in the current pipeline, need one penalty per type: a common
$\lambda$ is sensible only for samples "of similar sizes"
[@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 49].

:::


{{< pagebreak >}}

## From undirected to directed networks aka DAGs {.unnumbered .appendix}


Gaussian Bayesian networks orient edges under Markov and faithfulness
assumptions; interventions (Perturb-seq and related CRISPR screens)
supply the environments needed for causal claims
([Peters et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12167);
@svininCausalNetworkAnalysis2025). Any of them can generate a
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ for DeCovarT.

::: {#nte-separation .callout-note title="Graphical independence models"}



Glasso returns an **undirected** graph. Growing a gene panel by
neighbours is therefore not the same operation as blocking paths on a
DAG.

On a DAG, **$d$-separation** uses the direction of edges. A chain is
blocked by conditioning on the middle node; a collider is opened by
conditioning on the collision node (or on one of its descendants). On
an undirected graph, **$u$-separation** ignores direction: a path is
blocked when it meets the conditioning set. @fig-separation draws both.

```{.tikz}
%%| label: fig-separation
%%| fig-cap: Directed $d$-separation (chain blocked, collider opened), undirected $u$-separation on a minimal I-map, and the nesting of a Markov boundary inside a Markov blanket.
%%| filename: fig-cov-separation
%%| alt: Three panels. A is a chain A to B to C with B conditioned, so the path is blocked. B is a collider A and C both pointing at conditioned B, so the path is opened. C is an undirected graph on X: neighbours N1 and N2 form the Markov boundary, and a larger plate adds a non-neighbour E as a Markov blanket. O lies outside the blanket.
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=8mm and 11mm]
  \node[var] (a) {$A$};
  \node[obs, right=of a] (b) {$B$};
  \node[var, right=of b] (c) {$C$};
  \draw[edge] (a) -- (b);
  \draw[edge] (b) -- (c);
  \node[elabel, above=5mm of b] {A. Chain};
  \node[note, below=5mm of b] {blocked};

  \node[var] (a2) at (5.6,0.55) {$A$};
  \node[var] (c2) at (5.6,-0.55) {$C$};
  \node[obs] (b2) at (7.5,0) {$B$};
  \draw[edge] (a2) -- (b2);
  \draw[edge] (c2) -- (b2);
  \node[elabel, above=5mm of b2] {B. Collider};
  \node[note, below=6mm of c2] {opened};

  \node[var] (x) at (11.6,0) {$X$};
  \node[var] (n1) at (10.0,0.95) {$N_1$};
  \node[var] (n2) at (10.0,-0.95) {$N_2$};
  \node[var] (e) at (12.5,1.15) {$E$};
  \node[var] (o) at (13.3,-1.35) {$O$};
  \draw (n1) -- (x);
  \draw (n2) -- (x);
  \draw (e) -- (n1);
  \draw (o) -- (n2);
  \plate{boundary}{(n1)(n2)}{boundary}
  \plate{blanket}{(n1)(n2)(e)(boundary)(boundary-lab)}{blanket}
  \node[elabel, above=2mm of e] {C. Undirected};
\end{tikzpicture}
```
---

## Blanket versus boundary

A **Markov blanket** of a variable $X$ is any set $S$ that renders $X$
conditionally independent of the remaining variables
[@pearlProbabilisticReasoningIntelligent1988]. The neighbours of $X$ in
*some* undirected graph that is an I-map are always a blanket, but that
graph may contain redundant edges, so the neighbour set need not be
minimal.

A **Markov boundary** is a **minimal** Markov blanket. For a positive
distribution, that boundary is unique and equals the neighbour set of
$X$ in the **minimal undirected I-map**
[@pearlProbabilisticReasoningIntelligent1988;
@kollerProbabilisticGraphicalModels2009]. The boundary is therefore the
lower bound on the size of a blanket: every blanket contains a
boundary, and the boundary is the smallest one (@fig-separation, panel
C).
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}


::: {#nte-gbn-joint .callout-note}
## From a linear Gaussian Bayesian network to a joint normal

Order the $G$ genes along a DAG. A linear Gaussian Bayesian network
writes

$$
x_g=\mu_g+\sum_{g'\in\mathrm{Pa}(g)}\Lambda_{gg'}x_{g'}+\varepsilon_g,
\qquad
\varepsilon_g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_g),
$$ {#eq-gbn-local}

with $\Lambda_{gg'}=0$ unless $g'$ is a parent of $g$. In matrix form
$(\mathbf{I}_G-\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$
with $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ strictly triangular and
$\boldsymbol{Q}=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,\ldots,q_G)$, so

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=(\mathbf{I}_G-\boldsymbol{\Lambda})^{-1}\boldsymbol{Q}(\mathbf{I}_G-\boldsymbol{\Lambda})^{-\top},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=(\mathbf{I}_G-\boldsymbol{\Lambda})^{\top}\boldsymbol{Q}^{-1}(\mathbf{I}_G-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}).
$$ {#eq-gbn-joint-cov}

The precision has an edge between two parents of a common child
(moralisation), so a sparse DAG can give a denser $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$.
`bnlearn::gbn2mvnorm()` returns $(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$
from a fitted network [@R-bnlearn]. A DAG ground truth can therefore
populate type-specific $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ in simulations before
the bulk convolution. The dynamic counterpart is the Lyapunov
covariance of @nte-cov-lyapunov, whose precision need not follow the
edges of $\boldsymbol{A}$.
:::


## Other strategies to benchmark GRNs inference algorithms {.unnumbered .appendix}

Propsoed methods to benchmark GRNs inference algorithms are **inspired by**
GRETA [@badia-i-mompelComparisonEvaluationMethods2025] and BEELINE
[@pratapaBenchmarkingAlgorithmsGene2020].

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-metrics-families
%%| fig-cap: "Three core evaluation families for undirected cell-type GGMs. Perspectives that need a true skeleton, a DAG, extra assays, or perturbations are collected in this appendix."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone"}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["Estimated Omega_j"] --> B["Statistical robustness"]
  A --> C["Topology (undirected)"]
  A --> D["Knowledge-driven"]
  B --> B1["Technical bootstrap"]
  B --> B2["StARS-style instability"]
  B --> B3["KL, Hellinger, eBIC"]
  C --> C2["Degree, hubs, modules"]
  C --> C3["Concordance among estimators"]
  D --> D3["TF–target priors"]
  D --> D4["Pathway overlap"]
```


### Topological comparison {.unnumbered .appendix}

These describe **shape and concordance**, not correctness against a
true DAG. The core object is the undirected adjacency
$A_{gg'}=\mathbf{1}\{\hat\omega_{gg'}\neq 0\}$.

-   degree distribution and a power-law diagnostic (many biological
    networks are not strictly scale-free);
-   hub overlap across types (rewiring of hubs is a DeCovarT-relevant
    summary);
-   clustering coefficient, number of connected components, modularity;
-   overlap coefficients of edge **sets** between the three methods
    (intersection over the smaller set), which avoids punishing a
    method for returning a larger graph.

**Structural distances between two estimated undirected graphs** (no
true skeleton required) follow the `bnlearn` comparison helpers
([Comparing network structures](https://www.bnlearn.com/examples/compare-dags/)):

-   `hamming()` — Hamming distance: the number of edge additions and
    deletions needed to turn one skeleton into the other (no
    orientation term, because our graphs are undirected);
-   `shd()` — structural Hamming distance (SHD). For DAGs it also
    counts reversals; on undirected skeletons it reduces to the same
    add/delete count. Report both the raw distance and a version
    normalised by $G(G-1)/2$.

::: {#nte-metrics-viz .callout-note title="Visualisations"}

The aim is to **compare structure and inference**, not to decorate a
methods section. Each display should answer one question. Penalty-path
and `funkyheatmap` scoreboards live in the displays section of the reproducibility book; this section is about **supports, signs, and modules**.

**Supports and concordance (one type, one time)**

-   Binary adjacency heatmaps, genes ordered by a **common**
    hierarchical clustering (from a consensus distance
    $d_{ab}=1-\bar r_{ab}$ of methods, or from a biological
    ordering). Side-by-side heatmaps of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$
    for two types make rewiring visible; a third panel of
    $|\hat\omega^{(j)}_{gg'}-\hat\omega^{(\ell)}_{gg'}|$ is the
    differential-network view.
-   **Upset plots of edge presence** across `huge`, `SILGGM` and
    `PLNnetwork` at a fixed type $\times$ time: how many edges are
    unique to one estimator, shared by two, or shared by all three.
-   **Upset plots of edge sign**, which is stricter. An edge is a
    signed pair
    $\bigl(\{g,g'\},\operatorname{sign}(\hat\omega_{gg'})\bigr)$.
    Two methods can share the support and still disagree on the sign of
    the partial correlation; that disagreement is visible only in the
    signed Upset.
-   On-diagonal degree bars or a simple graph drawing **only** for a
    tiny TF subgraph; whole-transcriptome hairballs are not figures.

---

**Leiden modules from the precision weights**

Treat $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$ as a weighted undirected graph
with edge weights $|\hat\omega_{gg'}|$ (or
the partial correlation
$|\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}|=|\omega_{gg'}|/\sqrt{\omega_{gg}\omega_{g'g'}}$) on the selected
support. Cluster genes with Leiden
([`igraph::cluster_leiden()`](https://igraph.org/r/html/1.3.4/cluster_leiden.html)):
the weights enter the quality function directly, so modules reflect
**strength of conditional dependence**, not just binary adjacency.
Compare partitions across the three estimators (adjusted Rand index)
and across types (rewiring of modules). Do not feed the dense
$\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ into Leiden.

---

**Stability**

-   Edge-inclusion frequencies from the technical bootstrap as a
    heatmap or as a reliability curve (precision among edges with
    inclusion $>t$, as $t$ varies).
:::



<!-- ::: {#nte-metrics-true-skeleton .callout-note}
## :information_source: When a ground truth skeleton is available

On a simulator whose dependence we supplied
([S5, simulator](S5-misspecification.html#sec-s5-simulator)), or on a curated
Boolean skeleton used only as a **reference**, the usual ranking scores
apply to the **undirected** adjacency:

| Score | Definition on skeletons | Caveat |
|-------|-------------------------|--------|
| Precision / recall / $F_{1}$ or $F_{0.1}$ | TP, FP, FN against the reference skeleton | Needs a true or curated support; GRETA weights precision $10\times$ recall because inferred GRNs are sparse |
| Early precision | Precision among the top-$k$ edges | Robust when $k$ is the expected degree $\times G/2$ |
| AUPRC / AUROC | Ranking of edges | AUROC is too optimistic on sparse graphs; prefer AUPRC |
| Structural Hamming distance | Hamming / SHD against the true skeleton | Scale with $G$; report also normalised SHD |

Using a Boolean model (BEELINE curated networks; BoolODE) *as the prior* and a GGM *as the data-driven proposal* is a
legitimate consistency check; using the Boolean model *as*
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ would abandon the Gaussian convolution.

::: -->


**Literature / knowledge (observational, undirected)**

-   **Marker TFs**: is a known type marker present as a hub, or as a
    high-degree node in $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$ for that type?
-   **TF–target edges**: if $g$ is a TF and $g'$ a curated target,
    does the undirected edge $\{g,g'\}$ appear? Resources: CollecTRI,
    DoRothEA, and mouse TF catalogues — all incomplete.
-   **TF–TF via shared targets**: two TFs that share many neighbours
    may reflect a complex or an artefact of co-expression; report
    overlap with PPI / IntAct only as a soft score.


**Orthogonal multi-modal multi-omic assays**:

ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, and ATAC-seq (or multiome) networks are closer to
**physical interaction** than a partial correlation. They are
orthogonal, complementary modalities; they are **not** measured in the
core Suppinger scRNA-seq table we use for $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$. If a
later gastruloid multiome appears, GRETA is a possible evaluation
harness; SCENIC+ / CellOracle / Dictys remain out of the DeCovarT
**input**, because they return directed regulons, not SPD precisions.
The honest use is: project our undirected skeleton onto TF–CRE–gene
triples and score literature overlap; do not replace
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ with a regulon adjacency.



**Perturbation and interventional datasets**:

**CORNETO** [@rodriguezMierUnifyingMultisample2025] reformulates
knowledge-driven network inference as a joint constrained optimisation
problem (LP / MILP) over prior knowledge networks. It is **not** a
GGM. As a perspective scorer, it can take our data-driven support and
ask whether a sparse subnetwork of a PKN explains the omics under flow
/ Steiner / CARNIVAL constraints. That tests **mechanistic
plausibility**, not Gaussian fit.
